title: Film Music
objective: After this level you can explain how film scores shape what we feel.
summary: Silent films had live music. Jaws's two neighboring notes, E and F, stand in for a shark we rarely see. In a 2001 study, music changed how viewers read the same scene.

cards.headline: Silent films were never silent.
cards.body: Through the silent era, a pianist, a theater organist or, in big cities, a whole orchestra played live beside the screen. Before movies could talk, they already had music. So what is music doing to you while you watch?

cards.headline: Two notes, one shark
cards.body: For Jaws (1975), John Williams built the shark's theme from just two notes, E and F, alternating over and over. Remember Level 6? Two neighboring keys like E and F make a second, the kind of interval traditional theory counts as dissonant: tension with no release. As the shark closes in, the two notes grow louder and faster. You feel it coming before you see a thing.

cards.fact: In Jaws, the shark doesn't appear until the film's 81st minute.
cards.context: The mechanical sharks kept breaking down, so for most of the film the shark is suggested rather than shown. Williams's two notes do the work: hear them, and you know it's there. The score won him an Academy Award.

cards.headline: Same scene, different story
cards.body: In a 2001 study, people watched ambiguous film clips with upbeat music, gloomy music or none. With upbeat music, they read the scenes more positively; with gloomy music, more negatively; with no music, fairly neutrally. A week later, their memories of the clips leaned the same way as the music. A score doesn't just decorate a scene. It tells you what the scene means.

cards.headline: Film music: scored
learned: Silent films were accompanied by live music
Jaws: E and F alternating, louder and faster as danger nears
The theme stood in for a shark seldom seen
The same scene reads happier or darker with the music

questions.prompt: Films of the silent era were usually presented to audiences _____.

options.label: with live music in the theater
with music printed on screen
options.rationale: The music was played, not shown.

questions.explanation: A pianist, a theater organist or, in big cities, an orchestra played live beside the screen.

questions.prompt: In the 2001 study, match each soundtrack with how viewers read the scenes.
questions.explanation: With upbeat music, viewers read the scenes more positively; with gloomy music, more negatively; and with no music, fairly neutrally.

questions.prompt: The Jaws theme alternates E and F, two neighboring keys. What kind of interval is that?

options.label: An octave, the most consonant interval
options.rationale: An octave spans much further than one key.

options.label: A third, counted as consonant
options.rationale: Neighboring keys are closer than a third.

questions.explanation: Neighboring keys like E and F form a second, which traditional theory counts as dissonant: built-in tension.
